stories.moral: New routines become easier with support.
stories.moralExplanation: School brings new people and activities. Taking one step at a time and asking a trusted grown-up for help can make the day feel more familiar.

stories.title: Going to the Toilet

pages.lead: We pull up our pants.

pages.lead: We did it!

stories.moral: Listen to your body and ask for help.
stories.moralExplanation: Everyone learns bathroom routines at their own pace. We can notice what our body needs, ask for privacy or support, and wash our hands afterward.

stories.title: Going to the Doctor

pages.lead: First, we go to the doctor.
pages.body: The doctor will check how we are feeling and help us stay healthy.

animation.cue: First, we go to the doctor
animation.description: clinic exam-room entry: Boy with trusted adult steps through clinic doorway toward original doctor; then Boy takes next step and doctor gestures toward exam bench, same camera and room

frameCues: The doctor looks in our ears

pages.lead: We can tell the doctor how we feel.
pages.body: It is okay to ask questions.

animation.cue: We can tell the doctor how we feel
animation.description: clinic exam room: Boy points to tummy while looking toward doctor with thoughtful expression; then Boy gestures to simple feelings picture card while doctor nods and listens at his level

pages.lead: When we are done, we say thank you.

animation.cue: When we are done, we say thank you
animation.description: clinic exam-room doorway: Boy turns toward doctor and raises palm in grateful goodbye; then Boy lowers hand and takes step toward trusted adult at door, doctor smiles goodbye

stories.moral: It is okay to ask questions about your care.
stories.moralExplanation: A doctor helps us look after our bodies. We can tell a trusted grown-up how we feel and ask the doctor to explain what will happen.

stories.moral: Small daily habits help us care for ourselves.
stories.moralExplanation: Brushing helps keep our teeth clean. Practising regularly with support makes this routine easier to remember.

stories.moral: Patience and clear communication help us enjoy time together.
stories.moralExplanation: A restaurant can be busy and unfamiliar. We can ask for what we need, take turns, and get support if waiting feels difficult.

stories.moral: Staying together helps us navigate new places.
stories.moralExplanation: Airports have many people and steps to follow. Staying near our trusted grown-up and asking questions helps us move through the journey safely.

stories.moral: Play is happier when everyone feels safe and included.
stories.moralExplanation: We can take turns and notice how others feel. Asking for help when something feels unsafe helps everyone enjoy the playground.

stories.title: The Ant and the Grasshopper

pages.lead: On a sunny day, Ant gathered grain.
pages.body: Grasshopper played music in the meadow.

pages.lead: Ant carried seeds to her home.
pages.body: She was saving food for winter.

pages.lead: Grasshopper wanted to keep playing.
pages.body: He did not save any food before the cold days came.

pages.lead: Winter came, and food was hard to find.
pages.body: Hungry Grasshopper knocked on Ant's door.

pages.lead: Ant welcomed Grasshopper inside and shared her food.
pages.body: Grasshopper thanked her for being kind.

pages.lead: In spring, they gathered seeds together.
pages.body: They learned to plan ahead and help each other.

questions.question: Why did Ant save food?
What did the friends learn?

stories.moral: Plan ahead and help others with kindness.
stories.moralExplanation: Ant saved food for winter and still helped Grasshopper when he was hungry. Their friendship grew when they learned to prepare and work together.

stories.title: The Ant and the Pigeon

pages.lead: A little ant went to the river for a drink.
pages.body: A pigeon rested in a tree nearby.

pages.lead: Ant slipped into the water.
pages.body: Pigeon saw Ant struggling and wanted to help.

pages.lead: Pigeon dropped a leaf beside Ant.
pages.body: Ant climbed onto the leaf and floated toward the bank.

pages.lead: Ant floated on the leaf toward the riverbank.
pages.body: Thank you, Pigeon! said Ant. I will remember your kindness.

pages.lead: Later, Ant saw a hunter with a net near Pigeon.
pages.body: Ant nipped the hunter's ankle, and he dropped the net.

pages.lead: Pigeon heard the noise and flew away safely.
pages.body: Even a small friend can give great help.

questions.question: How did Pigeon help Ant?
What does this story teach us?
choices: Kindness can come back to us

stories.moral: Even a small friend can make a big difference.
stories.moralExplanation: Pigeon helped Ant with a leaf, and Ant later helped Pigeon escape danger. A kind action can matter regardless of how big or small we are.

stories.title: The Clever Crow

pages.lead: On a hot day, Crow was very thirsty.
pages.body: She flew over the meadow looking for water.

pages.lead: Crow found a pitcher beside a path.
pages.body: There was a little water at the bottom.

pages.lead: Crow put her beak into the pitcher.
pages.body: The water was too low for her to reach.

pages.lead: Crow stopped to think and noticed some pebbles.
pages.body: She picked up one small pebble in her beak.

pages.lead: Crow dropped the pebbles into the pitcher, one at a time.
pages.body: With each pebble, the water rose higher.

pages.lead: At last, Crow could reach the water and drink.
pages.body: Thinking carefully and trying patiently helped her solve the problem.

questions.question: What did Crow drop into the pitcher?
Why could Crow drink at the end?

stories.moral: Think carefully and keep trying.
stories.moralExplanation: Crow could not reach the water at first. By noticing the pebbles and trying a new idea patiently, she found a solution.

stories.title: The Tortoise and the Hare

pages.lead: Hare loved to talk about how fast he could run.
pages.body: Tortoise smiled and agreed to a friendly race.

pages.lead: The animals gathered to watch the race begin.
pages.body: Hare raced ahead while Tortoise took steady steps.

pages.lead: Hare looked back and saw Tortoise far behind.
pages.body: I have plenty of time, he thought.

pages.lead: Hare lay down under a tree and fell asleep.
pages.body: Tortoise kept walking, one step at a time.

pages.lead: Hare woke up and hurried toward the finish.
pages.body: Tortoise was already very close to the line.

pages.lead: Tortoise crossed the finish line first.
pages.body: Hare learned that steady effort matters more than boasting.

questions.question: Why did Hare stop running?
What helped Tortoise finish the race?

stories.moral: Steady effort helps us reach our goals.
stories.moralExplanation: Hare relied on being fast and stopped trying. Tortoise kept moving at his own pace and reached the finish through persistence.

stories.title: The Lion and the Mouse

pages.lead: A little mouse ran across a sleeping lion's paw.
pages.body: Lion woke up and looked down at Mouse.

pages.lead: Please let me go, said Mouse.
pages.body: One day, I may be able to help you.

pages.lead: Lion gently lifted his paw and let Mouse leave.
pages.body: Mouse thanked Lion for his kindness.

pages.lead: Later, Lion became tangled in a rope net.
pages.body: Mouse heard Lion calling and hurried to help.

pages.lead: Mouse chewed through the ropes with his little teeth.
pages.body: Soon, Lion could step out of the net.

pages.lead: Lion thanked his tiny friend.
pages.body: No one is too small to make a difference.

questions.question: How did Mouse free Lion?
What did Lion learn?

stories.moral: Treat others kindly, whatever their size.
stories.moralExplanation: Lion gave Mouse a chance to leave safely. Later, Mouse used his own special skill to help Lion, showing that everyone can contribute.

stories.title: The Fox and the Grapes

pages.lead: Fox walked along a sunny path.
pages.body: Soon, he came to a vineyard.

pages.lead: Fox spotted a bunch of purple grapes.
pages.body: They hung high above him on a vine.

pages.lead: Fox stretched up as far as he could.
pages.body: The grapes were still out of reach.

pages.lead: Fox jumped again and again.
pages.body: He could not reach the grapes and felt disappointed.

pages.lead: Those grapes are probably sour, Fox said as he walked away.
pages.body: But he had not tasted even one.

pages.lead: Fox sat down to think about what had happened.
pages.body: It is okay to feel disappointed without putting something down.

questions.question: Why could Fox not get the grapes?
Had Fox tasted the grapes?

stories.moral: Be honest about disappointment.
stories.moralExplanation: Fox could not reach the grapes, but that did not tell him how they tasted. We can admit that we feel disappointed without pretending something is worthless.

stories.title: The Dog and His Reflection

pages.lead: A baker gave Dog a bread roll.
pages.body: Dog happily carried it home in his mouth.

pages.lead: On the way, Dog crossed a wooden bridge.
pages.body: A quiet stream flowed below him.

pages.lead: Dog looked down and saw his reflection in the water.
pages.body: He thought it was another dog with another roll.

pages.lead: Dog opened his mouth to bark for the other roll.
pages.body: His own bread fell into the stream.

pages.lead: The bread floated away on the water.
pages.body: Dog realized there had been no other dog.

pages.lead: Dog rested on the grassy bank and thought about his mistake.
pages.body: He learned to appreciate what he already had.

questions.question: What did Dog see in the water?
Why did Dog lose his bread?
choices: He opened his mouth to bark
He shared it with a friend

stories.moral: Appreciate what you already have.
stories.moralExplanation: Dog mistook his reflection for another dog and tried to get more bread. He lost his own roll because he did not stop to understand what he was seeing.

stories.title: The Bundle of Sticks

pages.lead: A farmer's three children often argued.
pages.body: Their father wanted to show them how to work together.

pages.lead: Father brought a bundle of sticks tied with twine.
pages.body: He asked each child to try to break the whole bundle.

pages.lead: Each child tried bending the bundle.
pages.body: The sticks held together, and no one could break them.

pages.lead: Father untied the twine and separated the sticks.
pages.body: Now try one stick at a time, he said.

pages.lead: Each child could easily snap a single thin stick.
pages.body: They noticed how much stronger the bundle had been.

pages.lead: The family began helping one another in the garden.
pages.body: Like the sticks, they were stronger when they worked together.

questions.question: What was hard to break?
What did the family learn?

stories.moral: Working together can make us stronger.
stories.moralExplanation: A single stick bent easily, while the bundle held together. The family learned that helping one another made their shared work easier.

stories.title: The Enormous Turnip

pages.lead: Grandfather planted a little seed.
pages.body: Grow, little turnip, grow!

pages.lead: The turnip grew big, big, big!
pages.body: Grandfather pulled, but it stayed in the ground.

pages.lead: Grandmother came to help.
pages.body: Pull, pull! The turnip would not come out.

pages.lead: A child, a dog, and a cat joined in.
pages.body: Pull, pull! They needed one more helper.

pages.lead: A tiny mouse came to help too.
pages.body: They pulled together. Pop! Out came the turnip!

pages.lead: Everyone cheered for every helper.
pages.body: Even the smallest friend can help.

questions.question: What grew in the garden?
Who helped at the end?

stories.moral: Every helper matters.
stories.moralExplanation: The turnip came out when everyone pulled together, including the tiny mouse. Small contributions can help a group achieve something big.

stories.title: The Little Red Hen

pages.lead: Little Red Hen found some wheat seeds.
pages.body: Who will help me plant? she asked.

pages.lead: Not today, said Dog, Cat, and Duck.
pages.body: Hen and her chicks planted the seeds.

pages.lead: The wheat grew tall and golden.
pages.body: Hen and her chicks gathered the wheat.

pages.lead: Hen made flour and mixed the dough.
pages.body: Her chicks watched as she made bread.

pages.lead: Hen and her chicks enjoyed the bread they had made.
pages.body: The other animals wished they had helped.

pages.lead: Next time, Dog, Cat, and Duck helped plant.
pages.body: Working together made the job easier.

questions.question: What did Hen plant?
What did the friends do next time?

stories.moral: Shared work is a way to care for each other.
stories.moralExplanation: Hen and her chicks did many jobs to make their bread. The other animals learned to join in next time so the work could be shared.

stories.title: The Cap Seller and the Monkeys

pages.lead: A cap seller walked along a village path.
pages.body: His basket held red, blue, and yellow caps.

pages.lead: He rested under a shady tree.
pages.body: He kept his own red cap on his head.

pages.lead: When he woke, his basket was empty!
pages.body: Monkeys in the tree were wearing his caps.

pages.lead: The seller scratched his head.
pages.body: The monkeys scratched their heads too!

pages.lead: He took off his cap and put it down.
pages.body: The monkeys copied him and dropped the caps.

pages.lead: The seller put all his caps back in the basket.
pages.body: He smiled and waved goodbye to the monkeys.

questions.question: Who took the caps?
What did the monkeys do?

stories.moral: Pause and notice before solving a problem.
stories.moralExplanation: The seller saw that the monkeys copied his movements. Observing carefully helped him find a calm way to collect his caps.

stories.title: The Great Race

pages.lead: The Jade Emperor invited the animals to a race.
pages.body: Come across the river! he said.

pages.lead: Little Rat rode on strong Ox's back.
pages.body: Ox swam steadily across the quiet water.

pages.lead: At the bank, Rat hopped ahead.
pages.body: Rat came first, and Ox came second.

pages.lead: Tiger swam, Rabbit hopped, and Dragon flew.
pages.body: Each animal found a way to cross.

pages.lead: Goat, Monkey, and Rooster shared a raft.
pages.body: Horse, Snake, Dog, and Pig arrived too.

pages.lead: All twelve animals gathered at the finish.
pages.body: Their order became part of the Chinese zodiac calendar.

questions.question: Who came first?
Who carried Rat across the river?

stories.moral: Different strengths help us through challenges.
stories.moralExplanation: The animals crossed the river in different ways, and some worked together. We can value our own abilities and the help that others offer.

stories.title: Anansi and the Pot of Wisdom

pages.lead: Anansi the spider had a pot full of wisdom.
pages.body: Wisdom means knowing helpful things.

pages.lead: He wanted to keep the pot all to himself.
pages.body: He tied it in front of him to climb a tree.

pages.lead: The pot bumped against the tree.
pages.body: Anansi could not climb easily.

pages.lead: His little child had an idea.
pages.body: Try putting the pot on your back!

pages.lead: Anansi tried it, and climbing was easier.
pages.body: Someone else knew a helpful thing too!

pages.lead: Anansi came down to share his ideas.
pages.body: Everyone has something to teach and something to learn.

questions.question: Who had a helpful idea?
What did Anansi learn to do?

stories.moral: Everyone has something to teach and something to learn.
stories.moralExplanation: Anansi thought he knew everything, but his child offered a helpful idea. Listening and sharing let more people benefit from what we know.

stories.title: The Ugly Duckling

pages.lead: Some little birds hatched beside a pond.
pages.body: One fluffy gray bird looked different from the yellow ducklings.

pages.lead: The gray little bird wondered why he looked different.
pages.body: He wanted to feel that he belonged.

pages.lead: Mother Duck stayed close and comforted him.
pages.body: You deserve kindness just as you are.

pages.lead: The little bird grew through the seasons.
pages.body: His feathers and his long neck began to change.

pages.lead: In spring, he saw his reflection.
pages.body: He had grown into a young swan!

pages.lead: He swam with the swans and his duck family.
pages.body: Everyone belongs, however they look.

questions.question: What did the gray bird grow into?
Who deserves kindness?

stories.moral: Everyone deserves kindness and belonging.
stories.moralExplanation: The little bird felt different as he grew. He deserved care from the beginning, and growing into a swan did not change his worth.

stories.title: Goldilocks and the Three Bears

pages.lead: Goldilocks found a little cottage in the woods.
pages.body: She went inside without asking who lived there.

pages.lead: On the table were three bowls of porridge.
pages.body: One was too hot, one was too cold, and one was just right.

pages.lead: Goldilocks tried three chairs.
pages.body: The little chair wobbled, and she stood up carefully.

pages.lead: Upstairs, she found three beds.
pages.body: She lay on the little bed and fell asleep.

pages.lead: The bear family came home, and Goldilocks woke up.
pages.body: She realized she had used their things without permission.

pages.lead: Goldilocks said sorry and left with her grown-up.
pages.body: She learned to ask before entering a home or using someone else's things.

questions.question: Who lived in the cottage?
What should Goldilocks do before using others' things?

stories.moral: Ask permission before using someone else's things.
stories.moralExplanation: Goldilocks entered a home and used the bears' belongings without asking. Saying sorry and respecting other people's space helps repair mistakes.

stories.title: The Gingerbread Man

pages.lead: A baker rolled out dough and cut a little shape.
pages.body: The baker made a gingerbread man with bright buttons.

pages.lead: On the cooling tray, the gingerbread man opened his eyes.
pages.body: He smiled, stretched, and jumped down.

pages.lead: Run, run! he called as he ran through the garden.
pages.body: The baker watched to see where he would go.

pages.lead: A dog and a cat watched him hurry past.
pages.body: He waved hello as he ran along the path.

pages.lead: At a little stream, the gingerbread man stopped.
pages.body: He could not cross safely, so he thought about what to do.

pages.lead: He turned around and went back to the baker.
pages.body: His adventure taught him to stop and think before rushing ahead.

questions.question: Who made the gingerbread man?
What did he do at the stream?

stories.moral: Stop and think before rushing ahead.
stories.moralExplanation: The gingerbread man enjoyed his adventure but stopped when he reached the stream. Noticing a risk gave him time to choose a safer next step.

stories.title: The North Wind and the Sun

pages.lead: North Wind and Sun wondered who was stronger.
pages.body: Below them, a traveler walked in a warm coat.

pages.lead: Wind tried to blow the traveler's coat off.
pages.body: The traveler held it closed.

pages.lead: Wind blew harder and harder.
pages.body: The traveler wrapped the coat even more tightly around himself.

pages.lead: Then Sun had a turn.
pages.body: Sun shone gently, and the air grew warm.

pages.lead: The traveler felt warm and comfortable.
pages.body: He unbuttoned his coat and took it off.

pages.lead: Sun smiled, and Wind grew quiet.
pages.body: Gentleness can succeed where pushing harder does not.

questions.question: What did the traveler hold tighter when Wind blew?
Who made the traveler feel warm?

stories.moral: Gentleness can be more effective than force.
stories.moralExplanation: The stronger Wind blew, the tighter the traveler held his coat. Sun's gentle warmth helped the traveler choose to take it off himself.

stories.title: The Fox and the Stork

pages.lead: Fox invited Stork to share some soup.
pages.body: Stork was happy to visit her friend.

pages.lead: Fox served the soup in shallow plates.
pages.body: Fox could eat easily from his plate.

pages.lead: Stork's long beak could not scoop up the soup.
pages.body: She was still hungry, and Fox noticed her difficulty.

pages.lead: Another day, Stork invited Fox for a meal.
pages.body: She served the food in tall, narrow jars.

pages.lead: Stork could eat, but Fox could not reach inside his jar.
pages.body: Now Fox understood how Stork had felt.

pages.lead: They changed the dishes so both friends could eat.
pages.body: Good friends think about what each other needs.

questions.question: Why was the shallow plate difficult for Stork?
What helped both friends enjoy the meal?
choices: Using dishes that suited each friend

stories.moral: Think about what others need.
stories.moralExplanation: A dish that worked for one friend was difficult for the other. Changing the dishes helped both friends feel welcome and enjoy the meal.

stories.title: The Town Mouse and the Country Mouse

pages.lead: Country Mouse welcomed Town Mouse to his little home.
pages.body: The fields around them were quiet and green.

pages.lead: They shared a simple meal of seeds and berries.
pages.body: Town Mouse invited his friend to visit the town.

pages.lead: In town, there was a pantry full of tasty food.
pages.body: Country Mouse looked at the bread and fruit in surprise.

pages.lead: The two mice sat down to enjoy a feast.
pages.body: Then they heard footsteps at the pantry door.

pages.lead: A cat looked into the pantry.
pages.body: The mice waited safely behind a basket until the cat left.

pages.lead: Country Mouse chose to return to his peaceful home.
pages.body: He learned that feeling safe and content mattered more than a fancy meal.

questions.question: Where did Country Mouse feel most comfortable?
What mattered most to Country Mouse?

stories.moral: Choose what helps you feel safe and content.
stories.moralExplanation: Country Mouse enjoyed visiting but preferred the peace of his own home. A fancy meal was less important to him than feeling comfortable.

stories.title: The Honest Woodcutter

pages.lead: A woodcutter worked beside a quiet stream.
pages.body: His old iron axe helped him cut fallen branches.

pages.lead: The axe slipped from his hands into the water.
pages.body: The woodcutter sat on the bank, worried about his tool.

pages.lead: A woodland fairy appeared with a golden axe.
pages.body: Is this yours? she asked. No, said the woodcutter.

pages.lead: Next, the fairy showed him a silver axe.
pages.body: That is not mine either, he answered honestly.

pages.lead: Then she held up his old iron axe.
pages.body: That is mine! said the woodcutter with a happy smile.

pages.lead: The fairy returned his axe and gave him a gift for his honesty.
pages.body: The woodcutter thanked her and kept telling the truth.

stories.moral: Honesty helps people trust us.
stories.moralExplanation: The woodcutter told the truth even when he was offered something valuable. Being honest matters because it helps others understand and trust us, whether or not there is a reward.

questions.question: Which axe belonged to the woodcutter?
What did he do when offered the wrong axe?

stories.title: The Boy Who Cried Wolf

pages.lead: A shepherd boy watched sheep on a grassy hill.
pages.body: The villagers worked nearby.

pages.lead: One day, he called Wolf! as a joke.
pages.body: The villagers hurried up the hill to help.

pages.lead: There was no wolf, and the sheep were safe.
pages.body: The villagers asked the boy to call for help only when he meant it.

pages.lead: Later, a wolf appeared near the trees.
pages.body: The boy called for help, but the villagers were unsure what to believe.

pages.lead: The boy gathered the sheep into their strong pen.
pages.body: He kept calling clearly, and the villagers came to check.

pages.lead: The sheep were safe, and the boy said sorry for his joke.
pages.body: He learned to tell the truth and to rebuild trust through his actions.

stories.moral: Tell the truth so others can understand when you need help.
stories.moralExplanation: The boy's earlier joke made the villagers uncertain. Honest words and reliable actions help rebuild trust, and it is always okay to ask for help in a real emergency.

questions.question: Why were the villagers unsure at first?
What did the boy learn?

stories.title: The Fox and the Crow

pages.lead: Crow found a piece of cheese and sat on a branch.
pages.body: Fox noticed the cheese from the ground below.

pages.lead: What lovely feathers you have! said Fox.
pages.body: I am sure your singing is lovely too.

pages.lead: Crow felt proud and wanted to show off her voice.
pages.body: She lifted her head, still holding the cheese in her beak.

pages.lead: Crow opened her beak to sing.
pages.body: The cheese fell from the branch.

pages.lead: Fox picked up the cheese and walked away.
pages.body: Crow realized he had wanted her food all along.

pages.lead: Crow rested quietly and thought about what had happened.
pages.body: Next time, she would pause before acting on flattering words.

stories.moral: Think before acting on flattery.
stories.moralExplanation: Fox used praise to get Crow to drop her food. We can enjoy kind words while still thinking about what someone is asking us to do and whether it feels right.

questions.question: What fell when Crow opened her beak?
What can we do before acting on praise?
